rationale: A wins because it keeps the three real stories separated and refuses to staple unsupported causality onto them. Its cleanest move is warning that “the fact block pairs the two but never connects them,” which is exactly the discipline B loses when it calls the two-robot setup “the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format.” B has usable pieces, but it keeps trying to make the story bigger than the facts will carry.
gaps_in_A: “inflation coverage gives it immediate context” is plausible but still a soft peg; no live inflation story or competitor pricing context was supplied.
“Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory” is a useful beat frame, but it is external context, not a supplied fact.
The price angle could ask harder whether a flat-price pledge applies to delivery, regional menus, portions, and fees.
gaps_in_B: “the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format” is overclaiming. Digital Makeline is only being tested, and nothing says the two systems interact as one architecture.
“Other operators watching this decide their own capex from it” invents industry reaction. Maybe true, but not in the update.
“Half the prep time: what a guacamole robot actually does to a lunch rush” leans on wait-time and service-speed effects not supplied; it is a proof question, not yet a story.
“Run the detector first” is the wrong next step for a company announcement that already has three pitchable beats; prove the claims and fit-check reporters before hunting for a bigger peg.
